review_notes: I read the whole target file. I also read the neighbouring definitions and lemmas it uses: genusPrimeDiscriminants, genusFieldRoot_sq, the primeDiscriminantRadicand lemmas in Prime/Discriminants.lean, and the sibling MinusTwentyOne/GenusField.lean. I could not run Lean, so I don't know how the simp calls actually behave. The simp attribute on genusPrimeDiscriminants_neg_five looks sound: the hd argument appears in the left-hand side, so simp does not need to discharge it. The findings below are modest, concern the simp interface, and rest on reading the sources only.

findings.problem: To reduce `primeDiscriminantRadicand 5` to `5`, the proof unfolds the definition (`simp [..., primeDiscriminantRadicand]`). The existing simp lemma `primeDiscriminantRadicand_oddPrimeDiscriminant` only fires on `oddPrimeDiscriminant p`, which never matches the literal `5`. Simp therefore has no literal-level rule for odd prime discriminants. The literal even cases `primeDiscriminantRadicand_neg_four`, `_eight` and `_neg_eight` are also not `@[simp]`. The `-4` case a few lines earlier (`simp [hP]`) then depends on `primeDiscriminantRadicand_of_isEvenPrimeDiscriminant` plus a side-condition discharge. The sibling file repeats the unfolding (`norm_num [primeDiscriminantRadicand, ...]`), so every concrete discriminant needs its own unfolding of the `if`. The definition is exposed as an unfolding set instead of simp having a canonical normal form.
findings.proposed_change: Add a simp lemma stating that a prime discriminant which is not in `{-4, 8, -8}` is its own radicand. For example, `primeDiscriminantRadicand_of_not_even {D} (h : ¬ (D = -4 ∨ D = 8 ∨ D = -8)) : primeDiscriminantRadicand D = D`. Tag it `@[simp]` if `decide`/`norm_num` can discharge the side condition on literals. Also mark the literal lemmas `primeDiscriminantRadicand_neg_four`, `_eight` and `_neg_eight` as `@[simp]`. They give the same results as `primeDiscriminantRadicand_of_isEvenPrimeDiscriminant`, so they would not compete with it. Then this call can be `simp [hP]` and the definition need not be unfolded.
findings.benefit: The `-5` and `-21` genus-field files, and later discriminant examples, can reduce radicands of concrete discriminants with plain `simp`. Proofs no longer unfold the `if` in the definition, and the simp-normal form of `primeDiscriminantRadicand <literal>` is stable.

findings.problem: The identification of the candidate genus field with the explicit compositum is not a simp lemma, although the sibling `candidateGenusField_neg_twenty_one_eq` is tagged `@[simp]`. The prime-discriminant lemma `genusPrimeDiscriminants_neg_five` in this same file is `@[simp]`. The three `-5` pieces (prime discriminants, candidate field, finrank) therefore do not form a uniform simp interface. Any later `simp` call over `candidateGenusField hd` for `d = -5` will not reach `adjoin ℚ {I, √5}` automatically. The two files also differ in whether the squarefree proof is a named constant or an explicit argument. The `-5` file re-proves it inline on line 93, and the lemma takes `hd` as an argument.
findings.proposed_change: Make the statement uniform with the `-21` file, as it is likely to be reused by the neighbouring MinusFive modules. Either mark `candidateGenusField_neg_five_eq` `@[simp]` (its left side `candidateGenusField hd` has `hd` as a pattern variable, and the right side is a different head symbol, so it should not loop), or document why it is deliberately not simp. Optionally add a named `squarefree_neg_five` so that both lemmas can be stated without a hypothesis.
findings.benefit: The simp sets for the `-5` and `-21` genus-field examples would behave the same way. Downstream rewriting of `candidateGenusField` for `-5` would not need manual `rw [candidateGenusField_neg_five_eq hd]`.
